paper_title: RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Text-driven human motion synthesis has matured rapidly in recent years, driven by large-scale datasets paired with natural-language captions that enable models to learn rich semantic correspondences between text and motion [7, 12, 35, 4]. These advances have substantially improved the realism, controllability, and generalization of body-motion generation systems. Pure hand motion, however, has not progressed at the same pace. Yet, hands are the primary channel through which humans manipulate the world and convey nuanced intent. High-fidelity finger articulation is therefore essential for applications such as AR/VR avatars, teleoperation, sign-language synthesis, embodied agents, and dexterous robotics. From kinematic perspective, hands are uniquely challenging: they pack extremely high degrees of freedom into compact spatial region and exhibit frequent self-contact together with tightly coordinated inter-finger motion. Existing body-centric generators were not designed for this precision-intensive regime, and the lack of sufficiently large text-paired hand datasets has limited the communitys ability to systematically adapt modern generative architectures to dexterous hand motion. Table 1 and Figure 3 illustrate the sharp trade-off between scale and hand-motion fidelity in current datasets. Large-scale body-centric datasets [12, 38, 35, 4, 40] provide extensive motion diversity and textual supervision, but typically treat hands as rigid end-effectors with generic captions. In contrast, hand-object interaction and egocentric datasets [6, 1, 5, 11, 39] capture accurate contact dynamics and realistic manipulation behavior, yet rarely exceed few hours or include free-form language annotations. Existing pure-hand datasets [18, 13] similarly lack text supervision, limiting their usefulness for text-conditioned generation. More recent text-paired efforts such as BOTH2Hands [44], HandX [45], and the concurrent CLUTCH [31] begin to address this gap, but remain orders of magnitude smaller than modern body-motion corpora. Compounding this challenge, hand-motion generation demands substantially higher fidelity than full-body synthesis: subtle artifacts such as interfinger penetration or implausible coordination are immediately perceptible, yet are rarely captured by metrics designed for coarse body dynamics. To address this bottleneck, we introduce RoMo Hands: pure-hand, text-paired dataset containing approximately 542K in-the-wild motion sequences, corresponding to 884 hours and 95.5M frames at 30 fps, making it more than an order of magnitude larger than the next-largest pure-hand dataset. To ensure high-quality supervision, we design stringent automated filtering pipeline that removes nearstatic and low-information sequences, focusing the retained distribution on genuinely dexterous hand activity. Each clip is paired with five fine-grained captions at increasing levels of detail, describing atomic finger states, temporal dynamics, and spatial relations within hierarchical action taxonomy. Beyond the dataset itself, we establish comprehensive benchmark for pure-hand motion generation. Because leading generative architectures were originally developed for coarse-grained body motion, directly applying them to hands introduces substantial representational challenges. To bridge this gap, we propose novel redundant bimanual representation, Rhand, specifically designed for dexterous hand synthesis. Using this representation, we systematically adapt diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generation paradigms within unified benchmark setting. Under these evaluated adaptations, semantic and physical metrics yield different model rankings: strong text alignment does not guarantee kinematic plausibility or fine-grained physical consistency. These findings suggest that pure-hand generation introduces challenges beyond those typically encountered in conventional body-motion synthesis. Our core contributions are: RoMo Hands Dataset. large-scale, in-the-wild pure-hand motion dataset, an order of magnitude beyond existing pure-hand sets. Fine-Grained Captions. Five hierarchical captions per clip detailing finger articulation, temporal dynamics, and spatial relations, indexed under pruned RoMo [40] action taxonomy for stratified analysis. Bimanual Motion Representation. 393-dimensional hand representation (Rhand) that adapts the redundant body-motion paradigm to hands via synthetic root and inter-wrist heading. Pure-Hand Benchmark. comprehensive evaluation of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive architectures under documented hand-specific adaptations, exposing tension between semantic and physical quality. 2 Table 1: RoMo Hands provides an order-of-magnitude leap in hand-motion scale. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: We categorize prior work along three axes: (1) body-motion scaling paradigms; (2) hand-centric datasets and their scale constraints; and (3) generative architectures adapted to the bimanual domain. 2.1 Large-Scale Body Motion Datasets Text-to-motion research has transitioned from studio captures like AMASS [16] and HumanML3D [7] to massive, in-the-wild datasets such as Motion-X [12], MotionLib [35], and MotionMillion [4]. While these efforts scale body motion by orders of magnitude, they prioritize gross locomotion and treat hands as rigid end-effectors [12, 4, 40]. RoMo Hands imports the successful scaling recipe of RoMo [40], leveraging in-the-wild video and automated filtering to introduce the first body-scale, text-paired dataset devoted strictly to dexterous articulation. 2.2 Hand and Hand-Object Interaction Datasets disjoint line of work focuses on hands  (Table 1)  . Studio mocap datasets like InterHand2.6M [18], GRAB [29], ARCTIC [5], and OakInk2 [39] provide precise MANO [25] parameters but span only few hours and rarely include free-form text. Egocentric captures like GigaHands [6] and HoloAssist [34] broaden behavioral coverage but produce coarse annotations targeted at assistive agents rather than high-fidelity synthesis. Pure-hand text-paired datasets are nascent but have made crucial strides. BOTH2Hands [44] records 8.31 hours of motion, while HandX [45] unifies datasets via LLM-based annotation (54.2 hours). Concurrent to our work, CLUTCH [31] introduces an in-the-wild pure-hand dataset of 83 hours. These efforts establish the foundation for text-to-hand generation, yet they remain far below the scale required for the data-hungry architectures dominating the body domain. RoMo Hands provides this missing scaling engine with 884 hours, 542K sequences, and dense five-level captioning. 2.3 Text-Conditioned Motion Generation Generation has converged on three paradigms. Diffusion models (e.g., MotionDiffuse [42], MDM [30], PriorMDM [26], Kimodo [24]) iteratively denoise continuous sequences and lead the high-fidelity regime. Autoregressive models (e.g., T2M-GPT [41], MotionMillion [4]) predict discrete tokens over VQ-VAE or FSQ [17] codebooks. Finally, masked-token models like MoMask [8] and SnapMoGen [9] utilize bidirectional transformers for joint token generation. Multiple prior works target text-to-HOI [2, 3, 46], however, they rely on fixed object assets. For pure hands, CLUTCH [31] represents recent end-to-end system. However, it remains unclear how other generative architectures behave on the unique, high-DoF kinematics of hands. Rather than reinventing architectures, we ask how the existing models can be adapted. By bridging them with our novel representation (Rhand) and benchmarking on RoMo Hands, we isolate which body-centric design choices transfer to dexterous articulation and which require non-trivial adaptation. 3 Figure 2: The RoMo Hands curation pipeline. It extends the RoMo body-motion stack with three hand-specific stages: hand detection and bimanual MANO pose recovery (WiLoR), dexterity filter (detection-ratio + finger-articulation thresholds), and five-level VLM captioner (Qwen3.5).

sections.title: 3 The RoMo Hands Dataset and Representation
sections.content: 3.1 Collection and Captioning The RoMo Hands collection pipeline. RoMo Hands is built upon the data-collection and curation pipeline introduced by RoMo [40], which we rigorously repurpose for fine-grained pure-hand motion. The RoMo pipeline begins with multi-source web-video collection assembled via taxonomy-driven queries. They apply metadata filtering, scene detection, and single-human filtering, followed by semantic temporal segmentation against three-level action taxonomy. They then estimate 3D body motion in SMPL format for every retained clip using GVHMR [27], caption each segment using vision-language model, and finally prune the dataset with category-adaptive dynamic-score filter that removes static or low-activity sequences. Inheriting RoMos video pool, we extend this pipeline along three axes specifically targeted at hand motion failure modes. First, we introduce bimanual hand-pose stage that recovers per-frame MANO parameters using WiLoR [21] and reconciles them against the inherited wrist trajectory. Second, we enforce strict visibility threshold, discarding sequences where the mean per-frame WiLoR detection confidence falls below required per-hand minimum, ensuring the retained clips contain consistently visible hands rather than heavily occluded or off-screen artifacts. Third, we utilize Qwen3.5-27B [22] to caption each segment with five text descriptions at increasing levels of specificity, prompting the LLM to emphasize object manipulation context, temporal hand dynamics, and inter-finger spatial relationships. Figure 2 summarizes the end-to-end stack. Bimanual hand recovery. We recover hand motion using WiLoR [21], robust monocular bimanual hand estimator that performs per-frame hand detection and MANO [25] parameter regression in single pass. Each frame yields up to two hand instances, carrying left/right label, axis-angle wrist orientation, 15 finger-joint rotations, weak-perspective camera parameters {tcam, scam}, and detection score cached for downstream filtering. Because WiLoR lacks temporal component and assumes weak-perspective camera, per-frame wrist position and orientation suffer from frame-by-frame ambiguity: absolute depth is entangled with hand scale, and wrist orientation lacks shared anchor across frames. We resolve both issues via per-frame wrist anchoring step that reconciles WiLoRs wrist pose against the temporally consistent SMPL [14] wrist pose recovered by RoMos body pipeline. When the two estimates agree within configurable threshold, we average them. Otherwise, we trust WiLoRs wrist pose and solve inverse kinematics (IK) on the bodys arm chain to bring the SMPL wrist into agreement, locking both hands into the bodys temporally consistent world frame. For isolated frames where WiLoR fails to detect hand, we linearly interpolate the MANO parameters in axis-angle space between the nearest detections. This interpolation is reliable only for short gaps (up to 5 frames); longer gaps trigger segment split or discard. In aggregate, the hand-specific pipeline (bimanual recovery, plus the visibility and dexterity filters described next) retains 884 of the 1,238 inherited from RoMo [40], 29% reduction. Detection-ratio and dexterity filtering. Even after segmentation, two failure modes dominate the raw distribution: (a) clips where hands are barely visible due to occlusion or motion blur, and (b) clips where hands are visible but remain near static rest pose (e.g., resting at the side or statically holding an object). Training generator on these modes degrades quality by injecting regression noise or biasing the model toward the mean hand pose. We address this with two complementary filters. First, detection-ratio filter discards clips if the fraction of high-confidence WiLoR frames falls below per-hand minimum. Second, dexterity filter discards clips failing threshold that combines finger-articulation activity (mean joint-rotation velocity over the 15 finger joints) and inter-finger pose variation (mean pairwise ℓ2 distance between fingertip positions over time). Crucially, both filters run before captioning to preserve VLM budget and bias the final distribution toward dexterous, well-observed motion. Captioning at five granularities. Downstream tasks consume hand motion at varying detail levels as retrieval benefits from short headlines, and generation from paragraph-length descriptions. We therefore caption each clip at five progressive granularities via single structured prompt to Qwen3.527B [22], letting downstream models select supervision level at training time and enabling retrieval evaluation as function of caption complexity: L0 (headline): 24 word headline naming the action and salient object, e.g., hold volleyball. L1 (one-sentence scenario): short sentence placing the action in body and scene context, e.g., The woman holds volleyball in her left hand while standing on court. L2 (multi-sentence description): balanced description covering the active hand pose and the role of the passive hand. L3 (half-paragraph description): Adds finger-level articulation (palm orientation, finger curl) and brief temporal dynamics. L4 (full-paragraph description): The most verbose level, adding environmental context, fine wrist-and-finger detail, and inferred intent. Human validation. We audit caption fidelity and recovered-pose plausibility on 250 randomly sampled validation clips (50 per caption level). Twelve adult raters (ages 2050) with general technical backgrounds (at least bachelors degree), most without animation experience, viewed each source video beside its 3D reconstruction and assigned five-point Likert scores for overall action match, hand-specific captionmotion faithfulness, and reconstruction quality. Participation was uncompensated. The audit collected only technical judgments of the displayed artifacts and no personal or sensitive data; it did not constitute human-subjects research. Across 370 ratings, action match averages 4.16/5 (81% at least 4), captionmotion faithfulness averages 3.79/5 (66% at least 4), and reconstruction quality averages 3.53/5. The per-level breakdown in Table 11 shows that hand-specific caption accuracy remains within 3.703.96 across the five levels. The resulting vocabulary is analyzed in Section 3.2 and visualized in the right panel of Figure 4. Action taxonomy. We adopt RoMos three-level coarse-to-fine taxonomy (category sub-category atomic action) [40] and prune categories emptied by our visibility and dexterity filters; no new categories are introduced. We use the pruned taxonomy as stratification axis for evaluation, surfacing per-category model behavior that aggregate metrics hide (Figure 5). 3.2 Dataset Statistics and Coverage RoMo Hands totals 542K bimanual hand-motion sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps), with mean clip duration of 5.9 and an 85%/10%/5% train/val/test split at the segment level. The left panel of Figure 4 situates this scale against prior pure-hand and handobject datasets, placing RoMo Hands at 10.6 the duration of CLUTCH and 5.6 the caption count of HandX. To anchor activity coverage, we score GRAB [29] (1.1K seq., 2.86 h) and GigaHands [6] (12.7K seq., 16.40 h) under (a) Wrist log-density. (b) t-SNE feature views. Per-finger and per-joint dynamic scores, smoothness, autocorrelation, per-tier caption statistics, and side-by-side breakdowns against GRAB and GigaHands are available in the supplementary materials. 3.3 Bimanual Hand Motion Representation useful motion representation must faithfully encode skeletal kinematics while plugging cleanly into generative architectures. For body motion, standard templates utilize redundant joint-aware per-frame channels (position, velocity, and rotation) to improve the training signal across diffusion and autoregressive models. The 263-D HumanML3D representation [7] and the 272-D representation introduced by MotionStreamer [37] (subsequently adopted by MotionMillion [4], with public reference implementation by Xiao [36]) rely on low-dimensional heading frame followed by per-joint blocks. However, no analogous template has emerged for bimanual hand motion. Existing hand generators like CLUTCH [31] train on 198-dimensional MANO-derived representation that lacks the redundant velocity and heading-canonicalized channels that make body templates effective. We propose Rhand R393, which extends MANO into redundant per-frame template. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: The goal of this benchmark is to evaluate how state-of-the-art text-to-motion architectures that were originally designed for body motion generalize to pure hand motion when trained on large-scale, text-paired bimanual dataset. We adapt one representative model from each major generative family (diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive) to our shared Rhand representation, train them on the RoMo Hands split, and score them under matched semantic and physical metrics. 4.1 Evaluation Protocol We adopt the two-tier text-to-motion evaluation protocol of HumanML3D [7] and SnapMoGen [9], which was later adapted by CLUTCH [31] for bimanual hands. This protocol comprises semantic metrics scored by learned textmotion evaluator, and physical metrics computed directly on the 7 generated MANO meshes. Full metric definitions and hyperparameters for the TMR [20] evaluator are provided in the supplementary material. Semantic metrics. Following SnapMoGen [9], we utilize TMR evaluator trained on the RoMo Hands dataset. To ensure the evaluator scores articulation rather than spatial reconstruction, which would otherwise disproportionately reward VQ-style methods, we strip positions and velocities before normalization. We report: FID [10], measuring the distributional distance between generated and ground-truth (GT) motions; R-Precision (R@k) [7] for {1, 3, 10}, measuring the retrieval accuracy of the correct caption from pool of 32 captions (1 correct, 31 distractors drawn uniformly from the test set); MM-Dist, the average feature distance between generated motion and its paired text; CLIP score, the cosine similarity between generated motion and its paired text in the same TMR joint embedding space; Diversity, the variance across the generated set; and MultiModality, the variance of outputs generated from single repeated prompt. Physical metrics. To assess kinematic plausibility, we compute the following directly on the generated MANO meshes: Jerk (), which quantifies the temporal smoothness of the motion; Interhand penetration (), the percentage of frames where the left and right hand meshes intersect; Maximum self-hand penetration (), the worst-case collision depth within single hand (a depthvalued variant of the BimArt [43] self-penetration metric; see the supplementary material); and HF Power Ratio (), the fraction of velocity energy residing in the high-frequency band. The HF Power Ratio is speed-normalized, isolating high-frequency jitter from the overall motion velocity to complement the absolute Jerk metric. Test-set protocol. For each generator, we sample one motion per test prompt on the 17,348 RoMo Hands test clips of 40196 frames, the training length range. Sequence lengths are cropped to the nearest multiple of 4 to accommodate VQ tokenizer temporal downsampling. We apply the same type-aware normalization used during training, extract the essential features, and embed them via the frozen TMR evaluator. During each replication, we draw the conditioning caption uniformly at random across the five granularity levels (L0L4). Consequently, reported numbers are means marginalized over both replication noise and caption granularity. per-level breakdown is available in the supplementary materials. Ground-truth motions are processed through the identical pipeline to establish the reference distribution. Because the split is segment-level, we also remove every test clip whose source video appears in train and recompute the benchmark. The four-model ranking is preserved, with R@1 shifts between 0.026 and +0.009; Table 13 reports the full audit. We will additionally release strict source-video-disjoint partition with the dataset. Implementation details. We benchmark Kimodo [24] and MDM [30] (diffusion), MoMask [8] (residual-VQ masked-token), and MotionMillion [4] (FSQ-tokenized autoregressive). All four were originally proposed for full-body motion; we retrain each on RoMo Hands under the shared Rhand representation, frozen T5-v1.1-base text encoder [23], AdamW [15] optimization, and typeaware normalization, so any cross-architecture difference reflects representational fit rather than conditioning. Kimodo is held at its published medium configuration (the only change is the input/output dimension from SMPL features to Rhand); full per-model hyperparameters and schedules are in the supplementary materials. 4.2 Results We report semantic and physical results on the RoMo Hands test split in Table 3. Under the documented adaptations, the two metric families yield different rankings: MoMask and Kimodo lead the semantic metrics, while no single model universally dominates the physical metrics. Because MDM is prefix-conditioned, MotionMillion is evaluated at 150M rather than its published 1B scale, and MoMask Stage 2 had not fully converged, per-model rankings should be read as indicative rather than definitive. The supplementary covers all 40 categories of the pruned taxonomy. Physical results. The physical landscape inverts the semantic ranking. Kimodo is the cleanest overall with the lowest inter-hand penetration, the lowest HF power, and the best intra-hand jerk among baselines. MotionMillion incurs zero detected self-penetration and tracks GT HF power most closely, consistent with temporal regularization from its FSQ codebook. MoMask shows counterintuitive pattern: its acceleration sits well below GT yet its intra-hand jerk reaches 18 GT, slow-but-jagged signature consistent with abrupt residual-VQ token transitions that semantic metrics do not expose. MDM (DiP) has the highest contact violation rate under its evaluated 60-frame, 10-step configuration. This split between metric families is primary finding of the benchmark: no single evaluated configuration dominates both. The preferred configuration depends on whether downstream application prioritizes semantic text alignment or physical plausibility. This direction-level finding does not depend on treating the per-model ranking as definitive: pure-hand generation cannot be evaluated on semantic retrieval alone and requires complementary physical evaluation. The interactive statistics dashboard, side-by-side animated benchmark comparisons of every model on matched test prompts, and the 3D motion-grid visualizer are all available in the supplementary materials. We encourage the reader to inspect the comparisons in particular, since over-smoothing and high-frequency jitter are perceptually obvious in motion but only summarized in numbers here. Taxonomy-stratified results. Figure 5 shows the semantic metrics over the taxonomy categories and reveals blind spots that the aggregate Table 3 hides. The leader rotates across categories: MDM (DiP) sweeps the Communication category that has = 1660 samples; MoMask leads Performance Arts (n=324) and Assembly (n=162) on five of the six axes while MDM keeps the FID edge; and within Office (n=176) the rotation persists across metric families, with MoMask winning the retrieval cluster (R@1, R@3, R@10, CLIP) and MDM winning the distribution-matching axes (MM-Dist, FID). MotionMillion does not lead any category by mean, consistent with its aggregate performance. The full breakdown over all 40 categories, with semantic and physical-metric stratification, is available in the supplementary materials.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: RoMo Hands is an expansive in-the-wild dataset comprising 542K text-paired sequences across 884 hours. By pairing this scale with five-level hierarchical captioning scheme and coarse-to-fine taxonomy, we address the critical data bottleneck in dexterous motion synthesis. Our benchmark, underpinned by novel 393-D bimanual representation (Rhand), shows that body-motion generators exhibit distinct trade-offs under hand-specific adaptations. In particular, semantic and physical rankings diverge, and representation fit affects two different generator families. By releasing the dataset, taxonomy, and trained evaluator, we provide robust foundation for the next generation of text-to-motion research. Limitations. Sourcing in-the-wild video introduces residual noise from occlusions and motion blur, which we mitigate via filtering and evaluate through 250-clip human audit. The audit supports average caption fidelity and pose plausibility, but its five-point ratings are coarse and do not replace reconstruction error against ground-truth 3D hand pose. The dexterity filter introduces selection bias toward well-observed, active motion rather than the raw web-video distribution, and the dataset inherits the demographic and geographic composition of its public source pool. Retrieval metrics use single TMR evaluator trained on RoMo Hands, so they support relative comparisons under this shared evaluator rather than absolute comparison to body-motion benchmarks. Finally, the benchmark uses documented but non-identical adaptationsprefix conditioning for MDM, 150M MotionMillion decoder, and still-improving MoMask Stage 2so architecture-specific rankings are indicative rather than definitive. Future Work. Promising directions include scaling autoregressive decoders, such as pushing the MotionMillion [4] decoder to 1B+ parameters, as well as exploring cross-dataset transfer to complementary benchmarks such as HandX [45] and CLUTCH [31]. We also aim to integrate rich latent object context for hand-object interaction synthesis. Ultimately, this work paves the way for unified multimodal generator capable of jointly synthesizing body, hands, and facial expressions under shared tokenizer. Broader Impact. RoMo Hands accelerates research in AR/VR avatars, telepresence, and robotics. To mitigate misuse, we release strictly de-identified motion features and text annotations. However, as generative hand models mature, they could theoretically be combined with synthesized visuals to create misleading gestural content. We urge the community to employ responsible access controls and usage policies when deploying downstream applications.

sections.content: RoMo Hands: Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset Companion HTML files. set of HTML files accompanies this PDF and is best viewed in modern browser; each is self-contained and reproducible from the released dataset. We strongly recommend opening index.html first as it is single-page portal to every artifact below, with short descriptions and direct entry points into the interactive dashboards, the 3D motion grid, and the side-by-side generator comparisons that complement the static figures and tables in this paper. index.html: entry portal for the supplementary website; one card per artifact below with short description and direct link. RoMo_Hands_generative_method_comparison.html: side-by-side animation playback of ground-truth, MotionMillion, Kimodo M, MDM, and MoMask outputs on matched train, validation, and test prompts. Dataset_statistics.html: interactive statistical report covering durations, activity classes, per-finger and per-joint dynamic scores, inter-hand distance, smoothness, autocorrelation, and per-tier caption statistics, with cross-dataset comparison against GRAB and GigaHands. curated subset of these views is reproduced as static figures in Appendix A. Hand_motion_explorer.html: searchable, filterable card grid over 20-clip subset of RoMo Hands; each card opens full MANO viewer with timeline scrubber, the five-level captions, taxonomy labels, and per-clip quality scores. Hand_motion_example_grid.html: single-scene 3D viewer that plays the same 20 representative bimanual sequences in synchronized grid; clicking tile focuses it for scrubbing and inspection. RoMo_Hands_generative_method_benchmark.html: quantitative evaluation of every benchmark model, including taxonomy-stratified semantic retrieval (R@K, MM-Dist, CLIP), distributional metrics (FID, diversity), and physical plausibility. Scope. This supplement expands the main paper along five axes: extended dataset comparisons including body-only datasets that did not fit in the main table (Appendix A); the full specification of the bimanual hand motion representation Rhand, including channel layout, type-aware normalization, and comparison to alternative parameterizations (Appendix B); precise mathematical definitions of every semantic and physical metric (Appendix C); the complete result tables with 95% confidence intervals, additional baselines, and the per-caption-level Ground Truth breakdown (Appendix D); and per-model implementation details, training schedules, and scaling decisions (Appendix E). The main paper stands alone; this supplement is optional further reading for reproducibility and depth.

The pure-hand datasets in Table 1 top out at 83 (CLUTCH); the bodymotion regime, by contrast, has scaled by roughly two orders of magnitude in the last three years, from HumanML3Ds 28.6 workhorse [7] to Motion-X (144 h) [12], MotionLib (1456 h) [35], RoMo (1238 h) [40], and MotionMillion (2000 h) [4]. Joint positions are taken in the bimanual-canonical frame of Rhand (root-relative xz in the inter-wrist heading frame, world-absolute y; Section B.3), so δ is invariant to where the subject is in the scene and which way they are facing, and measures motion relative to the bimanual root. Joints aggregate arithmetically: per-finger score averages the three phalanges of that finger (no fingertips, 5 fingers 2 hands = 10 groups), per-hand score averages its 15 finger joints, and the per-clip overall score averages the 30 finger joints across both hands with the two wrists excluded; wrist scores are tracked separately over {0, 16}. We start from MANO and the body-motion-generation template, formalize the channel equivalence between R272 [37, 4, 36] and our Rhand, list the per-dimension layout, derive the type-aware normalization scheme, and compare to alternative bimanual parameterizations. B.1 From MANO to body-style representation MANO [25] parameterizes each hand by global axis-angle rotation rg R3, translation tg R3, 15 local joint rotations (R45), and 10 PCA shape coefficients β R10 (61 per hand, 122 bimanually). Existing hand generators [31] drop β and convert rotations to 6D continuous form [47], yielding the 99-D CLUTCH parameterization. Body-motion generators consume richer template: the HumanML3D 263-D [7] and 272-D [37, 4, 36] representations pack rotations alongside redundant root-relative joint positions, finite-difference velocities, and 6D heading frame, and this redundancy is what makes diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive backbones converge well. Our 393-D representation transports this template to MANOs 32-joint bimanual skeleton (16 joints per hand; wrist root and five three-phalanx finger chains, indices 015 left, 1631 right), uses 6D rotations throughout, and drops β since motion is generated at fixed mean shape. Two decisions distinguish it from naive port: (i) Heading is derived from the inter-wrist axis. Body representations canonicalize clip by aligning pelvis-anchored heading; hands have no natural pelvis. We extract yaw angle ψt from the wrist-to-wrist direction and apply Ry(ψt), rotation about the world-up axis only. Restricting heading canonicalization to yaw preserves the absolute y-component of every position, exposing world height as directly observable feature and avoiding the gravity-coupled rotations that would otherwise corrupt joint-position channels for two-handed gestures. (ii) The bimanual root is the wrist midpoint, not skeleton joint. We define rt = 1 + pR ) as the root used by the heading frame and the velocity channel. The vanilla recipe is empirically misapplied to ht for three independent reasons rooted in geometry, not data quality; the type-aware scheme is strict generalization that coincides with vanilla on benign representation but diverges on ht. Option A: vanilla per-channel z-score. This works on 263-D and 272-D body representations because every dimension is approximately Gaussian, well-conditioned, and geometrically unconstrained. None of those preconditions holds on ht: (i) Manifold-constrained channels. Each joints 6D rotation is not six free numbers but two 3-vectors that must remain unit-norm and mutually orthogonal; rescaling the six coordinates independently breaks both constraints, so the encoder no longer sees rotations as rotations. Concretely, the 6D rotation features (ωt and {ϕ(Rj )}, 192 + 2 = 194 active dimensions) live on the Stiefel manifold St(3, 2) (the first two columns of rotation matrix), carrying 332 + 1 = 97 true degrees of freedom in their 194 ambient dimensions. The redundancy is the price of continuity: Zhou et al. [47] prove that no continuous mapping Rn SO(d) exists below critical n, so the constraint a1 = a2 = 1, a1 a2 = 0 must be borne in the representation itself. After z-scoring this constraint no longer holds in the input the encoder sees, and the manifold structure has to be re-discovered from training samples rather than being baked into the representation. 20 (ii) Bimodal channels by construction. Several channels mix two regimes with very different scales (a one-shot draw at the start of each clip versus near-identity increment everywhere else, or the dual of that for velocities, where rare bursts coexist with long near-stationary runs), so single (µ, σ) fits neither, and after normalization the rare regime surfaces as 3050σ outlier that is in fact an entirely valid frame. The clearest case is the heading rotation ωt, which stores the absolute heading at = 0 (uniformly distributed on S1 across clips) and the incremental change at 1 (sharply peaked near identity, cos ψ 1, sin ψ 0). The dual pathology applies to the very-low-variance translation channels (root XZ velocity, joint velocities; 98 dims) on hand data, where most frames are near-stationary and σ is dominated by rare bursts; the result is occasional normalized values exceeding 30 on real validation data. (iii) Constant-by-construction channels. Four of the six heading dimensions carry no information at all (they are pinned to 0 or 1 for every frame of every clip) yet the standard σ max(σ, 1) guard rescales them as if they were random and the model has to learn that they are meaningless. Specifically, these are the third row of Ry(ψt) and the second columns y-component, which the yaw-only restriction pins by construction; their empirical σ collapses to 0, the max(σ, 1) guard kicks in, and the resulting channels become structured noise that the encoder has to explicitly learn to ignore. sections.content: Text-conditioned hand motion generation has no per-clip ground truth: many distinct motions can plausibly satisfy the same caption, so generated clip cannot be scored by direct reference comparison the way one would score reconstruction or denoising model. As consequence, no single metric and in particular no single physical metric is sufficient to declare motion physically plausible. Fol22 lowing the body-motion literature, we therefore triangulate with bank of complementary measures that fall into two families. Semantic metrics (Section C.1: FID [10], R-Precision@k [7], Matching Score, Diversity, MultiModality) operate in the latent space of the TMR [20] textmotion evaluator (Section E.4, trained on the 201-D essential subset of Rhand, Section B.6). They jointly measure (i) distributional alignment between generated and GT motions (FID), (ii) text-conditional alignment between motion and its prompt (R-Precision@k, Matching Score), and (iii) withinand cross-prompt variability (Diversity, MultiModality), so model cannot win all five simultaneously by collapsing to single mode or by ignoring the caption. Because every value is evaluator-specific, absolute numbers are not directly comparable to HumanML3D body-motion numbers; the reference ranges we cite from body-motion literature should be read as orientation, not as targets to clear. Throughout, Em and Et denote the TMR motion and text encoders. Physical metrics (Section C.2) are evaluator-free proxies computed directly on per-joint positions and posed MANO meshes. We borrow smoothness measures (Acceleration, Intra-hand Jerk, HF Power Ratio) and contact-validity measures (Interand Self-hand penetration variants) from the body-motion literature [7, 43], and add two hand-specific axes that we found necessary in pilots: bone-length violation rate, which catches token-by-token drift in autoregressive generators, and finger-flexion posture mean, which catches the flat hand failure mode. None of these individually proves motion is physically valid; together they flag the dominant failure modes we observed in pilots. The model is conditioned on 20-frame prefix and predicts the next 40 frames rather than generating the full 196-frame clip unconditionally; this collapses most of the multi-modal posterior and lets much shorter sampling schedule suffice. 8 layers, 8 attention heads, hidden dim 512, feed-forward 2048, dropout 0.1, GELU Architecture. activations, SDPA attention. The text condition is the full T5-v1.1-base token sequence cross-attended (via prefix tokens) into every layer. Per-channel loss weights match the representation: position dims (9104) get weight 2; root XZ velocity and height (02) get weight 10 (under-represented but high-impact for trajectory). Sequence shape. Fixed window of 20 frames context + 40 frames prediction = 60 total, with both ends pinned (min_seq_length = max_seq_length = 60). Inference requires prefix tensor (in practice: the ground-truth prefix from the eval pipeline). Diffusion. Cosine 50-step DDPM training schedule with variance fixed-small, CFG dropout 0.1, and CFG weight 2.5 at sampling. At validation we reduce to 10 DDPM steps: prefix-conditioned generation empirically needs an order of magnitude fewer denoising steps than the full-sequence variant. Optimization. AdamW, learning rate 3.27 104 (the batch-size-scaled paper baseline), gradient clip 0.5, EMA on (β = 0.999, update every 10 steps). Per-GPU batch 256 across 2 GPUs (effective batch 512). 200 epochs. Best val/loss = 0.04689 at epoch 74. Scale-down rationale. The 196 60-frame reduction is deliberate representation simplification, not compute compromise: when the model predicts only 40 frames given 20 frames of context, the DDPM posterior is far less multimodal and 10 denoising steps suffice. E.3.3 MoMask (residual VQ + masked transformer) MoMask [8] is 3-stage pipeline: (Stage 0) train residual VQ tokenizer that maps motion to discrete sequence; (Stage 1) train masked transformer that fills in masked tokens conditional on text; (Stage 2) train residual transformer that refines the higher-residual codes given the Stage 1 output. Stage 1 and Stage 2 are independent given frozen Stage 0 tokenizer and were trained in parallel on independent jobs. Stage 0: RVQ tokenizer. Convolutional encoder (down_t = 2, stride 2 token rate 7.5 Hz), 6-quantizer residual VQ with 512 codes per quantizer (per-quantizer codebooks, not shared), code dim 512, EMA codebook updates (µ = 0.99), 20% code dropout. 64-frame training window. Text-independent; AdamW, LR 2.83 104, no decay/EMA, step LR at iters {150K, 250K} with γ = 0.05. 200 epochs at single-GPU batch 2048. Reconstruction val/loss 0.026, codebook perplexity 156 (moderate utilization typical for first-stage VQs at this dataset scale). Stage 1: Masked transformer. Operates on quantizer 1. At each step cosine-scheduled fraction of tokens is replaced by [MASK] and the model predicts originals given remaining context and the text caption. Architecture: 8 layers, 6 heads, latent 384, FFN 1024, dropout 0.2, max length 55 tokens. Text is the full T5 sequence cross-attended into every layer; caption-drop 0.1. Optimization: AdamW, LR 3.46 104, step at iters {72K, 100K} with γ = 0.1, 1K linear warmup; 120 epochs at effective batch 1536 (7682 GPUs). Val/loss 3.79, accuracy 25.85%. Batch was scaled 1.5 over the H200 1.5-scaled LR; dropout was bumped from MoMasks 0.1 to 0.2 because the hand baseline with dataset is 5 smaller than HumanML3D (+1.5 pp val accuracy). torch.compile was disabled after observing recompile thrash from BERT-style mask-ratio sampling. Stage 2: Residual transformer. Operates on quantizers 26 conditional on the Stage-1 prediction. Same architecture as Stage 1 except: conditioning input is the Stage-1 token sequence (text still cross-attended), cond_drop_prob= 0.2, weights shared across the 5 residual heads. Optimization: identical schedule to Stage 1; val/loss 4.50, accuracy 10.39%. Stage 2 was still on slow downward slope at epoch 120 but the schedule was kept identical for parallel-launch simplicity; extending to 200 epochs would likely move accuracy to 1315%. Stages 1 and 2 share no weights and were trained in parallel on disjoint 2-GPU shards once the Stage-0 checkpoint was available. E.3.4 MotionMillion (FSQ tokenizer + LLaMA AR decoder) two-stage tokenizer + autoregressive language model, modeled after MotionMillion [4]. We trained the small (150M-parameter) variant. Stage 1: FSQ tokenizer. Finite Scalar Quantization [17] replaces MoMasks residual VQ; FSQ partitions low-dim latent into discrete bins per axis, sidestepping codebook collapse. Architecture: the same convolutional encoder as MoMasks Stage 0 (down_t = 2, token rate 7.5 Hz, width 512, depth 3, 64-frame window), with 5-axis FSQ at levels [8, 8, 8, 6, 5] for an implicit codebook of 15,360 tokens ( 30 MoMasks 512). Optimization: AdamW, LR 2 104, step at iters {150K, 250K} with γ = 0.05; 600 epochs at single-GPU batch 512. Val/loss 0.0171 at epoch 569, about 4 lower reconstruction loss than the MoMask Stage-0 RVQ, as expected for 30 codebook. Stage 2: LLaMA AR decoder. Causal LLaMA-style [32] model predicting the next FSQ token given (text, previous tokens). Architecture: 12 layers, 12 heads (no GQA), hidden 768, intermediate 2048, RoPE [28] θ = 10K, RMSNorm, SDPA. Max motion-token length 64 ( 8.5 s). Text condition is the full T5 sequence (180-token cap) cross-attended rather than concatenated, keeping the AR prefix short. CFG drop 0.1, CFG scale 2.5. Optimization: AdamW, LR 2.45 104 ( 1.5-scaled from the H200 baseline), weight decay 0.01, gradient clip 1.0, step at iters {30K, 60K} with γ = 0.1, 2K warmup; effective batch 1024 (1288 GPUs). torch.compile enabled on the inner LlamaModel only. Outcome: best val/loss 7.36 (accuracy 6.36%) at epoch 79 of 250-epoch budget with early stopping (patience 15 on val/loss); stop fired at epoch 154. Train accuracy at the best checkpoint was 58%, indicating the 150M variant overfits this dataset. The original MotionMillion uses 1B-parameter decoder; we started with 150M to de-risk the FSQ integration, and the train/val gap is the green light for capacity scale-up. 1B and 3B configs are checked in but untrained. E.4 Evaluation: TMR retrieval evaluator The TMR model [20] is the evaluator, not generator: once trained it is the canonical scorer for every text-to-motion model in this work via R@k retrieval and FID. Architecture. Dual encoder with shared transformer backbone, consuming the 201-D essential subset of Rhand (root frame + per-joint 6D rotations only; Section B.6). Both branches encode into 768-D joint latent space. 8 layers, 8 heads, FFN 3072, dropout 0.1, SDPA; T5-v1.1-base inline (256-token cap, bf16 buffer). Loss. Standard TMR combination: reconstruction (λrec = 1.0), motion-latent KL (λKL = 105), encoder regularization (λE = 105), textmotion latent alignment (λlatent = 105), and InfoNCE [33] contrastive across the batch (λNCE = 0.1, temperature 0.1). Unlike SnapMoGen [9], we do not use the threshold_selfsim = 0.80 paraphrase mask: in hyperparameter sweeps, removing the mask and using AdamW weight decay 0.01 (vs. SnapMoGens 105) gave the best R@1 by 34 pp on the held-out val set. Optimization. AdamW (β = (0.9, 0.99)), LR 2.5 104, weight decay 0.01, gradient clip 0.5 (tighter than diffusion models because contrastive loss is sensitive to spikes from hard negatives), 1500-step linear warmup, step LR at epochs {40, 60} with γ = 0.1. 100 epochs at effective batch 768 (384 2 GPUs); torch.compile enabled. Validation every epoch (rather than every 5) so the best-by-R@1 checkpoint is reliably captured. Val/loss 6.38 at epoch 98; the top-6 checkpoints across epochs 9399 are within 0.004 val/loss of each other. All retrieval-based metrics (R@k, FID, Diversity, MModality) in this paper are computed against this evaluator. E.5 Matched-budget scaling across architectures The cross-architecture comparison in Section 4.2 is comparison of representational fit between four generator families on the same data, not comparison of compute. To keep that comparison fair we sized every generator under two principles: (i) matched to the data: depth, batch, and schedule are tuned to RoMo Hands 85% train split rather than carried over from each methods body-motion default; and (ii) matched to one another: generator parameter counts are kept inside single decade ( 40M150M) so any ranking we report reflects how each architecture handles the bimanual representation, not raw capacity. Tokenizers (MoMask RVQ, MotionMillion FSQ) are exempt from (ii) because their objective is reconstruction quality and codebook coverage, not text-conditional generation; we keep them at their published sizes and let the codebook do the work. The headline consequence is the MotionMillion entry: its as-published 1B-parameter decoder would have been 7 larger than the next biggest generator and would have confounded the crossarchitecture comparison, so we trained the 150M variant in this work instead. Two clarifications. First, MoMask is reported as two rows because Stages 1 and 2 are independent transformers given the frozen Stage 0 tokenizer; they share the architecture and the schedule. The Stage 0 RVQ (10M params, 6512 codes) and the MotionMillion FSQ (12M params, 15.4K-token codebook) are kept at their published sizes for the reasons given above. Second, the MotionMillion train/val accuracy gap reported in Section E.3.4 ( 58%/6%) is the green light for revisiting the 1B and 3B configurations once the rest of the pipeline is locked, but doing so under fair-comparison protocol would also require pushing the other generators capacities up by comparable factor; we leave that scale-up to future work. E.6 Reproducibility The RoMo Hands dataset, the action taxonomy, the five-tier captions, the TMR retrieval evaluator, and the per-baseline training configurations and checkpoints reported in this paper will be publicly released through the project page under the licenses listed in Section F. Together with the architectures, optimizers, and training budgets documented in Section E, this release will allow any single result in Table 3 to be reproduced from the same starting point.
